name: Duane Wilkins
story: After completing a horticulture certificate, Duane Wilkins studied geography, environmental science and GIS mapping at the University of Waikato. His work has spanned health and conservation; at DOC he managed a team of map makers. He worked with Māori groups on Treaty of Waitangi investigations and taught local people in Iraq and Afghanistan to map roads, water, power and schools. At LINZ he worked in geospatial capability building. In 2020, he was seconded to the COVID-19 Operations Command Centre and developed a support website and map tools for Māori and Pacific communities and NGOs. In 2021, he led the Police ArcGIS Enterprise implementation team.

Wilkins recalls that Eagle Technology designed DOCgis before 2003, with departmental analysts and developers continuing its development. He also recalls difficult relations between regional teams and the GIS manager. He later returned to lead GIS at DOC; in 2012 the team became a shared service for the regions, a change he remembers as highly successful.

LINZ’s 2026 Geospatial Capability Committee page lists Wilkins as a corresponding member and identifies him as the geospatial consultant for Ngā Poutama Matawhenua’s Practical Māori GIS Mapping Wānanga webinar series. LINZ’s 2020/21 annual report records fortnightly online Ngā Poutama sessions from October 2020, delivered with Te Kāhui Manu Hōkai for iwi, Māori trusts and environmental groups.

LINZ’s school capability record lists Wilkins as a virtual field-trip subject specialist and Geographic Information Advocate for the 2017 virtual field trip. LINZ later featured him in Map My Wāhi virtual field trips for the East Coast and Taranaki, with material on StoryMaps, field data collection and local mapping.

The National Library of New Zealand credits Wilkins as creator of ArcFlax Edition 2.0 Whanganui, a 2006 interactive GIS data DVD. His later published resources include 2025 guides to historical imagery and 3D StoryMaps for kaupapa Māori GIS. In 2026, he wrote about two decades of Māori GIS practice, practitioner networks, and the importance of data authority and provenance.
